title: Framework to estimate the cost-effectiveness of the Genome Sequencing-based surveillance network: an integrated operational model-epidemiological model approach
abstract: Understanding how genomic surveillance capacity translates into population health outcomes is critical for designing effective pandemic response systems, yet the interaction between operational design and epidemiological dynamics remains insufficiently characterized. We develop an integrated analytical framework that links a whole-genome sequencing (WGS) – based surveillance network with a two – variant epidemiological transmission model to evaluate how surveillance operations influence variant detection, intervention timing, and health outcomes. The framework combines a modified susceptible – exposed – infectious – recovered – susceptible (SEIRS) model with a detailed operational representation of a centralized WGS surveillance network in India, incorporating sample collection, transport, batching, sequencing capacity, and reporting delays. We simulate 54 scenario combinations defined by three sequencing capacity levels, three sampling proportions, three variant emergence timings, and two variant profiles (high severity – high immune escape and low severity – low immune escape). Detection of a novel variant triggers a modeled intervention consisting of isolation of some diagnosed individuals, increased testing rates across disease states, and expanded access to hospitalization. Across simulations, the time from variant emergence to intervention implementation ranged from 73 to 351 days, depending on operational and epidemiological conditions. Increasing sampling proportion reduced detection time only when sequencing capacity was sufficient; under constrained capacity, higher sampling increased congestion and delayed detection. Expanding capacity from low to nominal levels substantially reduced turnaround times, with diminishing returns at higher capacity. Earlier detection consistently improved intervention effectiveness, with deaths averted ranging from 0.06% to 14.49% across scenarios. The cost per life – year saved ranged from INR 9,137 to INR 326,714 across all configurations, remaining below one to three times India ′ s GDP per capita, consistent with established cost – effectiveness thresholds. These results demonstrate that the performance of genomic surveillance systems is jointly determined by operational and epidemiological dynamics. Effective surveillance design, therefore, requires coordinated optimization of sampling strategies and sequencing capacity to enable timely intervention and maximize population health benefits.

summary.oneLiner: Simulations of India's genome sequencing network suggest earlier variant detection improves intervention effectiveness, and that sampling rate and sequencing capacity must be tuned together.
summary.overview: The paper builds a combined model linking an epidemic simulation of SARS-CoV-2 with a detailed operational model of India's centralized genome sequencing network. It tests how sampling proportion, sequencing machine capacity, and the timing of a new variant's emergence affect how fast the variant is detected and when public health interventions start. Detection time ranged from 73 to 351 days across scenarios, and earlier detection consistently improved outcomes. The authors estimate cost per life-year saved and conclude that whole genome sequencing plus intervention is cost-effective under their assumptions. Results are model-based and depend on many assumed parameters.
summary.question: How do sequencing capacity, sampling proportion, and variant emergence timing in a genomic surveillance network affect variant detection time, intervention timing, health outcomes, and cost-effectiveness?
summary.method: An integrated framework combining a modified two-variant SEIRS epidemiological model with an operational model of sample collection, transport, batching, sequencing, and reporting delays. The authors simulate 54 scenario combinations with uncertainty analysis (Latin Hypercube Sampling and repeated runs), and calculate cost per life-year saved as the mean of the ratio of net costs to life-years saved. Model parameters were calibrated to Indian data and some values were assumed or fitted.
summary.data: Calibration used OWID diagnosed-case data and excess death estimates for February to December 2021, GISAID sequencing and collection-to-submission time data from March 2020 to February 2022, and parameters from the literature. The scenarios are hypothetical simulations set in India, with three sequencing capacity levels (30, 60, 90 machines), sampling proportions of 5%, 10%, and 30%, and three variant emergence times.
findings: Time from variant emergence to intervention implementation ranged from 73 to 351 days across simulations, depending on operational and epidemiological conditions.
Increasing sampling proportion reduced detection time only when sequencing capacity was sufficient; under constrained capacity, higher sampling increased congestion and delayed detection.
Expanding capacity from low to nominal levels substantially reduced turnaround times, with diminishing returns at higher capacity.
Earlier detection consistently improved intervention effectiveness, with deaths averted ranging from 0.06% to 14.49% across scenarios.

Cost per life-year saved ranged from INR 9,137 to INR 326,714 across configurations, which the authors state is below one to three times India's GDP per capita, a WHO-style benchmark, so sequencing plus intervention is described as highly effective.

The authors describe whole genome sequencing with public health intervention as cost-effective across a range of scenarios, and note that the directional findings would hold even with more granular models.
summary.whyItMatters: The authors suggest that genomic surveillance design requires coordinated choices on sampling strategy and sequencing capacity, since adding capacity or sampling alone may not speed detection or be cost-effective. For public health planners in LMICs, the paper frames sequencing as a cost-effective investment, though the authors caution that results rely on assumed parameters and simulated interventions.
